a6271.speech: Has proposed the expansion of the G7 grouping of the world’s wealthiest countries to include India, Australia, South Korea and Russia.

a6271.speaker: S. Jaishankar, External Affairs Minister of India
a6271.name: S. Jaishankar
a6271.title: External Affairs Minister of India
a6271.speech: Underscored that India “can play a positive global role,” in the extraordinary situation spawned by the pandemic and stressed that India seeks to move toward NORMS, a ‘New Orientation for a Reformed Multilateral System’; outlining India’s priorities in the UNSC, he said: “We have always been a voice of reason and a votary of international law. We advocate dialogue, consultation and fairness in our approach to global issues. And we emphasize global development, addressing climate change and eradicating of poverty as central to planet’s future.”

a6271.speaker: Narendra Modi, Prime Minister of India
a6271.name: Narendra Modi
a6271.title: Prime Minister of India
a6271.speech: In Prime Minister Modi’s words, India’s work in the UNSC will be guided by 5Ss: Sammaan – Respect; Samwad – Dialogue; Sahyog – Cooperation; Shanti – Peace; and Samriddhi – Prosperity.

a6395.speaker: Elizabeth Kah, Executive Director of Journalists for Public Health and Development Initiative (J4PD), Bauchi
a6395.name: Elizabeth Kah
a6395.title: Executive Director of Journalists for Public Health and Development Initiative (J4PD), Bauchi
a6395.speech: Stated that for organizations to achieve impactful results, particularly Civil Society Organizations, strategic planning must be embraced to realize their objectives, mission and vision ; noted that the organization will put together a strategic and work plan that will improve accessibility to public health in Bauchi State in particular and the country as a whole working with relevant agencies ; according to her, as a guide, a strategic plan is valuable and must be diligently done in line with the set objectives of the organization.

a6395.speaker: Elizabeth Kah, Executive Director of Journalists for Public Health and Development Initiative (J4PD), Bauchi
a6395.name: Elizabeth Kah
a6395.title: Executive Director of Journalists for Public Health and Development Initiative (J4PD), Bauchi
a6395.speech: Commended the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) for collaborating with J4PD in the implementation of its activities in the state, assuring that the collaborative effort will yield positive and impactful outcome.

a6395.speaker: Rabi Ekele, Team Lead of USAID State2State
a6395.name: Rabi Ekele
a6395.title: Team Lead of USAID State2State
a6395.speech: Stressed the importance of a strategic plan for effective implementation of issues of health, education, water and sanitation as well as other public health issues ; said that J4PD being a dynamic organisation working in the public sector has a responsibility of getting adequate and accurate information that will create access to health, standard of education and water, sanitation and hygiene ; commended J4PD for putting together the workshop during which a strategic plan for impactful operations will be developed, urging the members to contribute to the exercise.

a6395.speaker: Mainas Ayuba, State Acting Chairperson, Disability Network Forum
a6395.name: Mainas Ayuba
a6395.title: State Acting Chairperson, Disability Network Forum
a6395.speech: Commended J4PD for the partnership with the Forum in the area of dissemination of useful information to the public about the state of vulnerable people in the state ; stressed that vulnerable people which include people with disabilities need special attention from government and other relevant institutions and agencies in order to get the required attention.

a6395.speaker: Grace Maikudi, Executive Director of LANGA Women
a6395.name: Grace Maikudi
a6395.title: Executive Director of LANGA Women
a6395.speech: Said that her organisation has enjoyed effective relationship with J4PD over the years, attributing the successes recorded to the collaborative effort, while commending J4PD for organizing the workshop, saying that it will go a long way in further strengthening the operations of the organization.

a6395.speaker: Usman Muhammad, Focal Person in the Ministry of Budget, Economic Planning and Multilateral Coordination
a6395.name: Usman Muhammad
a6395.title: Focal Person in the Ministry of Budget, Economic Planning and Multilateral Coordination
a6395.speech: Commended J4PD for its sustainable effort in reporting activities of the government in relation to Multilateral support.

a6459.speaker: Cllr. Tiawan Saye Gongloe, Liberian human rights lawyer and keynote speaker at World Press Freedom Day
a6459.name: Cllr. Tiawan Saye Gongloe
a6459.title: Liberian human rights lawyer and keynote speaker at World Press Freedom Day
a6459.speech: Called on Liberia's journalists to practice their vocation with distinction, realizing that “freedom of the press is not freedom from responsibility” ; said that even in the United States, which is regarded the forebear of human freedom, “we've seen how some major media outlets were sued by then former President Donald Trump for defamation” ; “While many of those cases were dismissed, a few led to settlements, corrections, and retractions—after it was shown that facts were misrepresented or recklessly reported” ; “What Liberian journalists must learn from this example is what happens when journalists get it wrong—when headlines are based on rumors rather than facts. When journalists engage in false reporting, the press risks loss of public trust. And without public trust, press freedom could crumble.”

a6459.speaker: Cllr. Tiawan Saye Gongloe, Liberian human rights lawyer and keynote speaker at World Press Freedom Day
a6459.name: Cllr. Tiawan Saye Gongloe
a6459.title: Liberian human rights lawyer and keynote speaker at World Press Freedom Day
a6459.speech: Admonished Liberian media to begin training journalists in AI and digital tools, not just to compete, but to lead in investigative reporting: “That is the spirit with which I speak on today on the sub-theme ‘Sustaining Independent Journalism and Press Freedom in the Digital Age' which was carved from the global theme: Reporting in the Brave New World: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Press Freedom and the Media” ; on the “bright side”, recalled that in 2016 the Panama Papers shook the world when over 11 million leaked documents exposed how world leaders and business elites were hiding wealth in offshore tax havens, a feat achieved only because investigative journalists used AI-powered tools and data-mining software ; “Let's look at an African case. Not long ago, BBC Africa Eye used metadata analysis, facial recognition, and hidden cameras to uncover the Sex for Grades scandal in Nigerian and Ghanaian universities. That report led to investigations, suspensions, and policy reform. Digital tools exposed injustice where silence had once prevailed” ; “That's the power of AI when used in the public interest. In Liberia, AI could be used as tool to help journalists dig deeper, work smarter, and hold individuals and institutions accountable—without fear or favor”, expressing the wish that Liberian journalists were using similar tools to trace how public funds meant for clinics in Grand Kru or schools in Bong mysteriously vanish.

a6459.speaker: Cllr. Tiawan Saye Gongloe, Liberian human rights lawyer and keynote speaker at World Press Freedom Day
a6459.name: Cllr. Tiawan Saye Gongloe
a6459.title: Liberian human rights lawyer and keynote speaker at World Press Freedom Day
a6459.speech: On “the dark side” of digital media, said that is when technology becomes dangerous, citing the Myanmar example where “Facebook's algorithms—powered by artificial intelligence—amplified hate speech and fake news targeting the Rohingya minority”, and said this digital disinformation fueled ethnic violence that resulted in mass displacement and atrocities the UN later called genocide ; in Liberia, he stressed, “if we don't control how hate speech and fake news spread through our own media platforms, we risk lighting fires we cannot put out” ; referenced the war between Russia and Ukraine, where AI-generated deep fakes—like a fake video of President Zelenskyy announcing surrender—go viral ; warned that when elections are approaching journalists should be vigilant: “One fake video could inflame ethnic tensions or destabilize a peaceful process.”

a6459.speaker: Cllr. Tiawan Saye Gongloe, Liberian human rights lawyer and keynote speaker at World Press Freedom Day
a6459.name: Cllr. Tiawan Saye Gongloe
a6459.title: Liberian human rights lawyer and keynote speaker at World Press Freedom Day
a6459.speech: Called on journalists to establish ethical standards for technology use in the media, ensuring truth remains the highest goal, and to uphold self-regulation, not self-destruction, saying journalists must police themselves with integrity before others are forced to do so ; “On World Freedom Day, 2025, I call on all Liberian journalists in Liberia and around the world, to recommit themselves to the kind of journalism that promotes peace, understanding, national unity, progress and prosperity, not the journalism that promotes hate and division” ; “Journalism must be used to bring light to corruption, not confusion to the people. Journalism must be used to help in promoting the building of clinics, classrooms, and trust—not fear, hatred, and doubt” ; made it clear that press freedom is not a gift from government, nor the privilege of journalists: “It is the right of the people to know the truth as guaranteed by article 15c of the Constitution of Liberia, to question authority, and to shape the future of Liberia” ; said that when exercised responsibly, journalism becomes one of the more powerful and effective instruments of national transformation.

a6459.speaker: Cllr. Tiawan Saye Gongloe, Liberian human rights lawyer and keynote speaker at World Press Freedom Day
a6459.name: Cllr. Tiawan Saye Gongloe
a6459.title: Liberian human rights lawyer and keynote speaker at World Press Freedom Day
a6459.speech: Recalled that over the past thirty-six years he has stood with journalists and media institutions—defending them at police stations, in courtrooms, at the Ministry of Justice, and through his writings and public advocacy: “I have experienced, both personally and professionally, what it means to fight for the right to speak truth in the face of power. In that journey, I have not only been a lawyer for the press—I have at times been a witness, a participant, and yes, a victim in the defense of this sacred right” ; “But I believe that freedom of the press is not a weapon—it is a tool. And it must be wielded with responsibility, not recklessness. That is why, during my tenure as Solicitor General of Liberia in 2009, I made a conscious decision not to use Liberia's anti-speech laws—sedition, criminal malevolence, and criminal libel against the President—to silence journalists. Instead, I drafted the legislation that would later become the Kamara A. Kamara Act of Press Freedom, repealing those oppressive laws. I submitted that draft to the President of Liberia, with a copy to the then-Secretary General of the Press Union of Liberia, Mr. Peter Quaqua” ; “That act was not just a legal reform—it was a principled stand. A stand for a Liberia where the press is free to challenge authority, but also called to a higher duty: to inform, to unite, to elevate” ; “Let me be clear: I do not wish to associate myself with mercenary journalism—the kind that sells headlines for personal gain, spreads lies that divide families, and stirs hatred instead of hope. I want to stand with a press that contributes to the building of Liberia—a press that helps bring better education, health care, food sufficiency, infrastructure, electricity, and telecommunications.”

a6548.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF), World Bank and Reserve Bank of Malawi (RBM) (data)
a6548.name: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a6548.title: World Bank and Reserve Bank of Malawi (RBM) (data)
a6548.speech: According to data sourced from these institutions, Malawi’s economic hardships over the last five years under the Malawi Congress Party (MCP) have been tough to bear: real GDP growth slowed from an average of 4.1% between 2011–2019 to just 2.2% since 2020, dipping to 1.8% in 2024, outpaced by population growth of 2.6%; annual inflation spiked to 25-34% in 2022–2023, easing to around 28% in 2024; the kwacha depreciated from MWK814/US$ in 2021 to MWK1,683 in 2023 and roughly MWK1,733 by end-2024; the fiscal deficit fluctuated between -2.9% in 2023 and -7.9% of GDP in 2024, while public debt peaked at over 80% of GDP in 2024.

a6548.speaker: World Bank
a6548.name: World Bank
a6548.speech: Warns that climate change could shave 3-9% off GDP by 2030, and up to 16-20% by 2040-2050, if climate adaptation isn’t accelerated.

a6548.speaker: Polls surveys
a6548.name: Polls surveys
a6548.speech: Based on polls surveys, Peter Mutharika is seen as a ‘Man of the Moment’ in this election, despite attempts to discredit him over his age.

a6649.speaker: Department of Trade and Industry of South Africa (notice issued in May with a 60-day comment period)
a6649.name: Department of Trade and Industry of South Africa (notice issued in May with a 60-day comment period)
a6649.speech: Issued a notice that goods imported from Israel and manufactured in the Israeli-occupied territories ought to be labelled as such ; the notice sets out the government's position clearly: "The government of South Africa recognises the state of Israel only within the borders demarcated by the United Nations in 1948. Such demarcated borders of Israel by the UN do not include Palestinian territories occupied after 1967." ; the department said that to comply with the act's trade description requirements, any goods - not just from Ahava - manufactured within the UN-defined occupied Palestinian territory and imported into South Africa cannot be labelled as "Made in Israel".

a6649.speaker: The Inkatha Freedom Party, the African Christian Democratic Party, the South African Zionist Federation and the Shembe Church ("Africans for Israel")
a6649.name: The Inkatha Freedom Party
a6649.title: the African Christian Democratic Party, the South African Zionist Federation and the Shembe Church ("Africans for Israel")
a6649.speech: Marched to the trade and industry department's head office in Pretoria to demand that minister Rob Davies withdraw the notice.

a6649.speaker: Kenneth Meshoe, ACDP leader
a6649.name: Kenneth Meshoe
a6649.title: ACDP leader
a6649.speech: According to him, the notice "is discriminatory, indefensible and part of the international boycott, divestment and sanctions campaign to isolate and delegitimise Israel."

a6649.speaker: Mangosuthu Buthelezi, IFP leader
a6649.name: Mangosuthu Buthelezi
a6649.title: IFP leader
a6649.speech: Added that Davies' action is yet another indication that the South African government has taken Palestine's side in the conflict, and claimed that the notice had no basis in law ; "Our government has maintained an unstated position with regards to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, and has made no effort to conceal the fact that it supports the Palestinian cause. One seldom hears an unbiased statement in Parliament. Our government has taken sides."

a6649.speaker: Mangosuthu Buthelezi, IFP leader
a6649.name: Mangosuthu Buthelezi
a6649.title: IFP leader
a6649.speech: Likened the consumer boycotts against the re-labelling to those preceding the persecution of Jews and the Holocaust in Germany.

a6649.speaker: Open Shuddah Street (pro-Palestine lobby group)
a6649.name: Open Shuddah Street (pro-Palestine lobby group)
a6649.speech: Responding to Thursday's protests, accused the IFP and ACDP of misleading their members and maintained that the notice upheld the law and consumers' rights to accurate information.

a6649.speaker: Open Shuddah Street (pro-Palestine lobby group)
a6649.name: Open Shuddah Street (pro-Palestine lobby group)
a6649.speech: According to the group, the trade description on Israeli cosmetics company Ahava's products was misleading because it did not correctly describe the place or country of origin - the goods are labelled "Made in Israel" whereas they originated from the Israeli-occupied territories - and it threatened to take the government to court if it did not order a re-labelling.

a6649.speaker: Cosatu (trade union)
a6649.name: Cosatu (trade union)
a6649.speech: Criticised the protest and appealed to Shembe Church spiritual leader Phakama Shembe not to allow the church's members to be co-opted into furthering "the racist supremacist ideology" of the SA Zionist Federation.

a6649.speaker: Patrick Craven, Cosatu spokesman (statement)
a6649.name: Patrick Craven
a6649.title: Cosatu spokesman (statement)
a6649.speech: "Those who choose to (participate in the protest) are either genuinely misinformed, opportunistic or are deliberately sacrificing principle on the altar of cheap politicking, as is being consistently demonstrated by the leader of the ACDP, Reverend Meshoe, and the IFP."

a6649.speaker: Palestine Solidarity Group, Passop (refugee-rights group), Kairos (religious leaders group) and the South African boycott, divestment and sanctions campaign
a6649.name: Palestine Solidarity Group
a6649.title: Passop (refugee-rights group), Kairos (religious leaders group) and the South African boycott, divestment and sanctions campaign
a6649.speech: At a Thursday press conference in Cape Town, voiced support for Davies' decision to issue the notice.

a6649.speaker: Mary Kluk, chairwoman of the SA Jewish Board of Deputies
a6649.name: Mary Kluk
a6649.title: chairwoman of the SA Jewish Board of Deputies
a6649.speech: Said the board and the SA Zionist Federation met Davies to discuss their concerns over implications of the notice and would, as invited, make a submission to the department.

a6715.speaker: Madalitso Kambauwa Wirima, Malawian Minister of Basic Education
a6715.name: Madalitso Kambauwa Wirima
a6715.title: Malawian Minister of Basic Education
a6715.speech: Extended Malawi government's “profound gratitude” to British High Commissioner Fiona Ritchie for the role she played in fostering strong partnership between the two countries, describing her work as remarkable: “High Commissioner Ritchie has served with professionalism, candour, and a genuine spirit of partnership that has left a lasting and positive impact across many sectors. From supporting Malawi’s public sector reforms to championing cultural exchange and inclusive development, she has been a steadfast and trusted friend of Malawi. As this occasion marks her final King’s birthday celebration in Malawi, we thank her deeply for her unwavering commitment to strengthening UK–Malawi relations and wish her every success in the next chapter of her distinguished career.”

a6715.speaker: Madalitso Kambauwa Wirima, Malawian Minister of Basic Education
a6715.name: Madalitso Kambauwa Wirima
a6715.title: Malawian Minister of Basic Education
a6715.speech: Highlighted that in celebrating King Charles III’s birthday, Malawians should reflect on the numerous activities he has personally undertaken “to serve humanity throughout his whole life — not only to the people of the United Kingdom but also to the world at-large, more especially to developing Commonwealth Member States like Malawi” ; “The King’s service to humanity is also demonstrated through his passion for combating climate change. He began addressing this issue at the young age of 21 in 1970 when he delivered his first major speech, in which he warned about the dangerous effects of plastic pollution.” ; emphasised that King Charles’ “foresight in 1970, when climate change was not widely recognised as a critical issue, is now at the core of the global agenda [with] countries like Malawi having first-hand experience of the devastating effects of climate change” ; “If the international community had seriously heeded His Majesty’s warning and taken appropriate actions, the world might not be in its current state. As Head of the Commonwealth, His Majesty the King continues to play a crucial role in promoting The Commonwealth’s core values; ‘democracy, human rights, good governance, the rule of law, multilateralism, and world peace’.”

a6715.speaker: King Charles III, British monarch (quoted by Minister Kambauwa Wirima)
a6715.name: King Charles III
a6715.title: British monarch (quoted by Minister Kambauwa Wirima)
a6715.speech: ‘In the present times, we are faced with a variety of environmental challenges. The growing pile of plastic waste is becoming a serious threat to our planet’s health. If we do not act now, we risk inflicting irreversible damage on our ecosystems’.

a6715.speaker: Madalitso Kambauwa Wirima, Malawian Minister of Basic Education
a6715.name: Madalitso Kambauwa Wirima
a6715.title: Malawian Minister of Basic Education
a6715.speech: Said King Charles’ “life and legacy would be incomplete without reflecting on the longstanding historical bonds of friendship that have existed between Malawi and the United Kingdom for over a century. Last year, Malawi proudly celebrated 60 years of independence, a significant milestone that was peacefully granted by the British Government. Malawi, then known as Nyasaland, became a British Protectorate in 1891. The influence of the United Kingdom has been profound and far-reaching, shaping our nation’s journey in numerous ways. On the momentous day of 6th July, 1964, Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II graciously sent Prince Philip, the Duke of Edinburgh, to celebrate Malawi’s independence, marking the end of colonial rule and the beginning of a new chapter for our nation. The cultural exchanges between our nations have left an indelible mark on Malawi. Our language, with English as an official language, our education system, legal structures, and even aspects of our dress and cultural practices bear the imprint of our shared history. The tremendous transformation of Malawi from a colonial territory to a vibrant, independent nation cannot be recounted without acknowledging the pivotal role played by Britain.” ; took cognizance of the involvement of the Malawi Defence Force in King Charles’ coronation as “a powerful symbol of the deep bonds of respect and friendship that define our relationship”, and of UK support in revitalising the Lake of Stars Festival, which “is a testament to our shared belief in the transformative power of culture and the arts” ; “These moments continue to build a people-to-people partnership that goes beyond policy and into the heart of our shared experience.”

a6715.speaker: Madalitso Kambauwa Wirima, Malawian Minister of Basic Education
a6715.name: Madalitso Kambauwa Wirima
a6715.title: Malawian Minister of Basic Education
a6715.speech: “Over the years, Britain has remained Malawi’s major development partner, increasing its official development assistance. British support covers all critical sectors of our society, including health, education, macro-economic stability, climate change, governance, and public financial management, among others. This support complements the government’s efforts in providing social services and addressing bottlenecks along the country’s development trajectory.” ; highlighted that in public financial management the UK is supporting the delivery of inclusive economic growth by building an economy that works for everyone, including “leveraging UK expertise in tackling unsustainable debt” ; “The UK is also supporting the government’s reform drive to establish robust public institutions capable of delivering high-quality public services. While applauding His Majesty’s Government’s continued support to Malawi, we are cognizant of the fact that sustainable development can only be achieved through enhancement of trade and investment. In this regard, we are grateful to the British Government for the support towards improving the business enabling environment for investors and exporters, and leveraging UK institutions – such as British International Investment – to provide reliable, sustainable investment. This support greatly complements the government’s current initiative of promoting investments in critical sectors of agriculture, tourism and mining as well as, other areas like manufacturing, energy and infrastructure development.”

a6715.speaker: Fiona Ritchie, British High Commissioner to Malawi
a6715.name: Fiona Ritchie
a6715.title: British High Commissioner to Malawi
a6715.speech: Alluded that “as a friend, supporter and ally of Malawi” she worries about the concerns raised by many Malawians across all walks of life of their fears of violence marring September 16: “My worry is compounded by the fact that my own country knows the trauma, cost and damage that politically driven violence causes, how quickly it can spill out of control and how long it can take to build back together.”

a6715.speaker: Madalitso Kambauwa Wirima, Malawian Minister of Basic Education
a6715.name: Madalitso Kambauwa Wirima
a6715.title: Malawian Minister of Basic Education
a6715.speech: Concluded her speech saying: “As we look ahead to the upcoming electoral period, the Government of Malawi remains firmly committed to ensuring a peaceful, transparent, and credible process. We share your concerns, High Commissioner, about the need to guard against political violence, and we welcome the continued support of the UK and other partners in reinforcing peace, civic education, and electoral integrity.”

a6786.speaker: Darrell Boyd, Chief Executive Officer of the Tulu Moye Geothermal Project
a6786.name: Darrell Boyd
a6786.title: Chief Executive Officer of the Tulu Moye Geothermal Project
a6786.speech: On how geothermal power works: "A geothermal power plant works by tapping into steam or hot water reservoirs underground; the heat is used to drive an electrical generator. Most geothermal plants are located in the western United States, where hot water reservoirs are common. Geothermal energy is heat derived within the sub-surface of the earth. Water or steam carries the geothermal energy to the Earth's surface. Depending on its characteristics, geothermal energy can be used for heating and cooling purposes or be harnessed to generate clean electricity. The supply of geothermal energy is limited and confined to certain areas only. The entire resource of geothermal energy is fairly bigger than that of coal, oil and gas."

a6786.speaker: Darrell Boyd, Chief Executive Officer of the Tulu Moye Geothermal Project
a6786.name: Darrell Boyd
a6786.title: Chief Executive Officer of the Tulu Moye Geothermal Project
a6786.speech: On Ethiopia's potential capacity: "Ethiopia's potential to the sector is very huge. Ethiopia does have a potential of producing 10,000 mw of power from geothermal. Ethiopia is among the few countries in Africa with a significant amount of geothermal resources, these resources are found scattered in Ethiopia's rift valley area and in the Afar Depression." ; "Demand for energy is going to increase and with the increase in population and extinction of non renewable source. More over today the government also supports the resource which is cleaner and do not spoil the environment. Geothermal energy can be made more widely available."

a6786.speaker: Darrell Boyd, Chief Executive Officer of the Tulu Moye Geothermal Project
a6786.name: Darrell Boyd
a6786.title: Chief Executive Officer of the Tulu Moye Geothermal Project
a6786.speech: On the Tulu Moye project: said operations of Tulu Moye Geothermal Project (TMGO), one of the first independent energy companies in Ethiopia, kick off drilling on 04 March 2020 at its project site in the Arsi Zone of Oromia Region, Iteya District, marking the beginning of the development of a 150 MW geothermal power plant in two phases with an anticipated total investment of USD 800 million, considered a breakthrough event by both government and project owners; by February 2023 the company looks forward to generating 50 MW in the first phase and by 2025 the project will generate 150 MW towards the Ethiopian Electricity Grid base-load needs. Said TMGO was established on 17 December 2017 and signed a power purchasing agreement with Ethiopian Electric Power on 19 December 2017, that it is a shareholding company of the Paris-based investment firm Meridiam SAS and the Icelandic Geothermal Development Company Reykjavik Geothermal, and that the exploration of three wells at Tulu Moye has been partially funded by GRM (Geothermal Risk Mitigation).

a6786.speaker: Darrell Boyd, Chief Executive Officer of the Tulu Moye Geothermal Project
a6786.name: Darrell Boyd
a6786.title: Chief Executive Officer of the Tulu Moye Geothermal Project
a6786.speech: On whether such partnerships can increase the country's power generation capacity: said the project is to generate and sell power to Ethiopian Electric Power for the next five years, that it is the first of its kind in Ethiopia and one of the means of attracting foreign direct investment, capacity building and expertise; Tulu Moye is one of the first licensed by the Ethiopian Energy Authority, along with Kobati Abaya and Aluto Langano. Said the project "brings the preeminent international geothermal scientists to Ethiopia, including from USA, Iceland & Kenya, in a great example of international and African regional cooperation at its best. The vision of the Ethiopian Government leaders to develop their vast geothermal resources, by partnering with international scientific expertise and private sector financing, has become a reality."

a6786.speaker: Darrell Boyd, Chief Executive Officer of the Tulu Moye Geothermal Project
a6786.name: Darrell Boyd
a6786.title: Chief Executive Officer of the Tulu Moye Geothermal Project
a6786.speech: On investing in Ethiopia: "May be the current situation of the country can be said difficult to invest, but if you are committed in your job it will be easy, we are operating in Oromia Region which is said to be one of the hardest places to invest because of the current political atmosphere of the country. We may face a little challenge but that can't even be taken as a challenge, we have a good relation with the Oromia regional offices and with the people around the village." Said that for the last twenty five years the government has been doing good work on attracting investment, making proclamations to create the legal, legislative and regulatory framework to allow private investment into the sector, and that as the first mover the company is working together with the Ministry of Finance, Ethiopian Electric Power, the Ministry of Water and Irrigation and other stakeholders: "It is super exciting to be the first, to set the way and develop the frame work and develop the sector to those who wants to follow, we are going to sell the power to Ethiopian Electric Power governing by the agreement and the geothermal proclamation and the public private proclamation."

a6786.speaker: Darrell Boyd, Chief Executive Officer of the Tulu Moye Geothermal Project
a6786.name: Darrell Boyd
a6786.title: Chief Executive Officer of the Tulu Moye Geothermal Project
a6786.speech: On geothermal as a business: "It is a long term profit business, but the profit is good. The sector needs a huge amount of money to start. It needs a lot of work to start the operation." ; "It depends on the three factors, its demand, supply and its competitiveness among other renewable resources in terms of cost, availability, reliability and so on. Totally it may take up to ten years to be profitable, but it is stable business. It can be made more widely available if the methods and technologies used to extract it are improved."

a6806.speaker: Trump administration
a6806.name: Trump administration
a6806.speech: has labeled USAID as an institution influenced by "left-wing extremists"

a6806.speaker: Elon Musk, key advisor on government spending
a6806.name: Elon Musk
a6806.title: key advisor on government spending
a6806.speech: has suggested that this suspension could potentially lead to the permanent closure of USAID, which has been a major player in global humanitarian aid since its inception in 1961 under President John F. Kennedy.

a6806.speaker: Somali government
a6806.name: Somali government
a6806.speech: has expressed grave concern over the potential consequences of the aid cut.

a6806.speaker: A senior official (anonymous, Somali government)
a6806.name: A senior official (anonymous
a6806.title: Somali government)
a6806.speech: emphasized that USAID's support has been instrumental in improving the living conditions of many Somalis, particularly in the areas of health and nutrition. "The loss of this support will be devastating for our people," the official stated.

a6806.speaker: Local aid organizations in Somalia
a6806.name: Local aid organizations in Somalia
a6806.speech: have sounded the alarm, with many fearing that the suspension of USAID funds will lead to further instability.

a6806.speaker: Humanitarian groups and foreign governments (international community)
a6806.name: Humanitarian groups and foreign governments (international community)
a6806.speech: have called on the U.S. to reverse its decision, warning that the suspension of aid will only exacerbate the already dire situation in Somalia. Many fear that the decision could set a dangerous precedent for future U.S. foreign aid policy.

a6806.speaker: Ken Jackson, a senior official at USAID
a6806.name: Ken Jackson
a6806.title: a senior official at USAID
a6806.speech: characterized the suspension as a "complete halt," signaling that operations in Somalia and other countries would be severely affected.

a6806.speaker: Humanitarian organizations
a6806.name: Humanitarian organizations
a6806.speech: stress that without a steady stream of foreign aid, Somalia will struggle to address its numerous challenges.

a6986.speaker: Tanzania Demographic and Health Survey 2022 (THDS-MIS) figures
a6986.name: Tanzania Demographic and Health Survey 2022 (THDS-MIS) figures
a6986.speech: Show that the rate of teenage pregnancy in Lindi and Mtwara regions has fallen to 25 percent, compared with 42 percent in 2015/2016, placing the regions second nationally behind Tabora and Kigoma, which stood at 45 percent respectively.

a6986.speaker: Ashura Ausi, Mtwara Regional reproductive and child health coordinator
a6986.name: Ashura Ausi
a6986.title: Mtwara Regional reproductive and child health coordinator
a6986.speech: Says reproductive health education has produced positive results to a large extent: “In 2023, teenage pregnancies were 0.2 percent of all pregnant women, but in 2024 they fell to 0.02 percent.” ; says reproductive health education has reached primary schools, secondary schools, colleges, health facilities and the community as a whole, enabling young people to obtain accurate information and knowledge ; says Mtwara previously had many challenges, including teenage pregnancies, young people not understanding their own bodies, an increase in sexually transmitted infections, unsafe abortions and even deaths ; “We were dealing with absenteeism from school, especially during menstruation, incorrect use of family planning methods and misconceptions about those methods.”

a6986.speaker: Ashura Ausi, Mtwara Regional reproductive and child health coordinator
a6986.name: Ashura Ausi
a6986.title: Mtwara Regional reproductive and child health coordinator
a6986.speech: Says the region has prepared a strategy aimed at providing reproductive health education to young people, including students, through special rooms at health facilities ; says emphasis has been placed on using teachers who have received special training in collaboration with non-governmental organisations ; says 57 government workers and nine from the USAID Afya Yangu project have received special training in order to teach reproductive health matters in a friendly and open way for young people ; says some schools provide special sessions for young people which have helped increase their understanding of protecting themselves from teenage pregnancy and sexually transmitted diseases.

a6986.speaker: Ashura Ausi, Mtwara Regional reproductive and child health coordinator
a6986.name: Ashura Ausi
a6986.title: Mtwara Regional reproductive and child health coordinator
a6986.speech: Says some wards have not been reached with services because of a shortage of reproductive health professionals and a lack of financial resources ; says the Government has set aside a budget for the construction of special rooms at health facilities to provide youth-friendly education, and that in 2025 the Government in Mtwara region expects to rehabilitate and improve the Likombe, Nagaga and Masasi health centres for that service.

a6986.speaker: Rabia Rashid (19), resident of Chimbuko village, Tandahimba district, Mtwara region
a6986.name: Rabia Rashid (19)
a6986.title: resident of Chimbuko village, Tandahimba district, Mtwara region
a6986.speech: Says she began using family planning methods after receiving education at school: “I was taught about reproductive health when I was in Form Two in science class. After that I went to a pharmacy and had an injection (three-month protection) for Sh3,000 because I was afraid of going to the dispensary and being seen.” ; says she used the injection for two years but found it was harming her health, so she switched to the natural calendar method, and after not being careful in counting her cycle she ended up becoming pregnant.

a6986.speaker: Abdallah Vitus, bodaboda (motorcycle-taxi) driver in Mtwara town
a6986.name: Abdallah Vitus
a6986.title: bodaboda (motorcycle-taxi) driver in Mtwara town
a6986.speech: Says there are girls who use implants, pills and injections as family planning methods: “Right now many use P2 or the one-off injection. Others are advised by bodaboda drivers so that they don't get pregnant,” he claims, explaining that some of those drivers buy the drugs for them or persuade them to use them when they are in a relationship, while carrying them to school free of charge.

a6986.speaker: Safia Haji (16), resident of Mnyundo village, Mtwara Rural district
a6986.name: Safia Haji (16)
a6986.title: resident of Mnyundo village, Mtwara Rural district
a6986.speech: Says she began using the injection after being advised by her friend without going through a professional: “My friend told me that the injection prevents pregnancy, so I went to a pharmacy and had the injection. After one month I began to menstruate continuously, and I was told to take pills to stop the bleeding.”

a6986.speaker: Subira Mwinyimkuu, resident of Magomeni, Mtwara town
a6986.name: Subira Mwinyimkuu
a6986.title: resident of Magomeni, Mtwara town
a6986.speech: Says some girls have been using long-term family planning methods such as implants: “You find someone who is 16 years old and has never given birth but has a five-year rod. Doctor, how do you insert a rod in someone who is not yet even self-reliant? I myself started using protection after giving birth.” ; says girls rush to protect themselves against pregnancy but do not pay attention to protecting themselves against sexually transmitted diseases and infections, including HIV.

a6986.speaker: Hasnath Shafii, resident of Mtama, Lindi region
a6986.name: Hasnath Shafii
a6986.title: resident of Mtama, Lindi region
a6986.speech: Says she was given an injection at the urging of her elder sister out of fear of becoming pregnant.

a6986.speaker: Health worker (name withheld), Mtama health centre
a6986.name: Health worker (name withheld)
a6986.title: Mtama health centre
a6986.speech: Says many girls are brought in by relatives or parents: “We cannot refuse them the service because the parent or guardian tells you openly: 'If you don't give this child the injection, I cannot afford to raise her together with her child'.”

a6986.speaker: Dr Thea Ntara, Special Seats Member of Parliament
a6986.name: Dr Thea Ntara
a6986.title: Special Seats Member of Parliament
a6986.speech: Spoke in Parliament on June 3, 2025 about the indiscriminate use of emergency contraceptive pills (P2) when contributing to the Ministry of Health's revenue and expenditure estimates for 2025/26; citing research by experts from the Aga Khan Hospital and Muhimbili University of Health and Allied Sciences (Muhas), she explained that incorrect use of P2 can cause serious health harms such as changes in blood circulation, stroke, paralysis, reproductive cancer, repeated miscarriages, and even sexually transmitted diseases.

a6986.speaker: Research by experts from Aga Khan Hospital and Muhimbili University of Health and Allied Sciences (Muhas)
a6986.name: Research by experts from Aga Khan Hospital and Muhimbili University of Health and Allied Sciences (Muhas)
a6986.speech: Cited as showing that incorrect use of P2 emergency contraceptive pills can cause serious health harms such as changes in blood circulation, stroke, paralysis, reproductive cancer, repeated miscarriages, and even sexually transmitted diseases.

a6986.speaker: Dalia Chimpota, parent from Chimbuko village
a6986.name: Dalia Chimpota
a6986.title: parent from Chimbuko village
a6986.speech: “A child may have reached puberty two years ago and the parent does not know; other times the parent is surprised to find she has already started using family planning methods. This is contributed to by parents' fear of talking to their children,” asking that education be provided to parents so they can help their children by giving them the right advice.

a6986.speaker: Fadina Chivanga, chairperson of Misri hamlet, Chimbuko village
a6986.name: Fadina Chivanga
a6986.title: chairperson of Misri hamlet, Chimbuko village
a6986.speech: Says girls have learned to use family planning methods out of fear of becoming pregnant.

a6986.speaker: Rashid Yusuph, chairman of Mnyundo village
a6986.name: Rashid Yusuph
a6986.title: chairman of Mnyundo village
a6986.speech: Says the ward development officer has been providing reproductive health education and the result has been a decline in teenage pregnancies ; “Many use injections, implants and pills, but not under pressure from a parent. It is their own decision after reaching an age of understanding.” ; says they have also been including young men in family planning education in order to help reduce pregnancies and unsafe sex ; says that despite the success in reducing teenage pregnancies, the challenge of indiscriminate family planning use still needs to be examined in depth: “Continuous education for young people, parents and the community as a whole is important so that such use is safe, correct and by consent arising from understanding, and not from fear or outside persuasion.”

a6986.speaker: Salama Mshamu, attendant at a pharmacy in Tandahimba
a6986.name: Salama Mshamu
a6986.title: attendant at a pharmacy in Tandahimba
a6986.speech: Says most customers are girls who are afraid to go to hospital for fear of meeting people who know them: “They come here out of fear; they are afraid of being seen. Here they get it in secret and no one asks them many questions.”

a6986.speaker: Emmiliana Woisso, family planning specialist and health worker, Marie Stopes Hospital
a6986.name: Emmiliana Woisso
a6986.title: family planning specialist and health worker, Marie Stopes Hospital
a6986.speech: Says the use of family planning methods causes no harm if it follows the advice of health professionals: “When a problem occurs such as continuous bleeding, we advise changing the method in order to help correct the body's hormones.” ; cautioned girls and women who have never had children and who use family planning without a doctor's advice, explaining there is a possibility of delay in becoming pregnant when they later want children ; “It is important to follow professional advice before starting to use any family planning method. There are clinical tests that need to be done to determine which method suits a particular person's body.” ; says someone planning to use more than one method at the same time should undergo a health examination to determine hormone levels rather than serving themselves directly at pharmacies without professional guidance.

a6986.speaker: Zuhura Mbuguni, Coordinator of Family Planning Services, Ministry of Health
a6986.name: Zuhura Mbuguni
a6986.title: Coordinator of Family Planning Services, Ministry of Health
a6986.speech: Says it is an offence in law for pharmacies to provide family planning injection services, even if some of their attendants have been trained, and that it should be provided at health facilities: “It is an offence in law to provide family planning services at pharmacies. If an attendant is caught, action will be taken against them. The only services they can provide are pills and condoms. Injections should be provided at dispensaries or health centres.” ; urged young people using family planning methods to follow procedure by going to health facilities so that they receive correct education from qualified professionals ; said indiscriminate use can cause health harm because every type of family planning has its own procedure and specific guidance: “There are some methods that may appear safe but if used improperly bring harm to the body.”

a6986.speaker: Zuhura Mbuguni, Coordinator of Family Planning Services, Ministry of Health
a6986.name: Zuhura Mbuguni
a6986.title: Coordinator of Family Planning Services, Ministry of Health
a6986.speech: Says they have concentrated on providing education in Lindi and Mtwara regions, where customs and traditions have contributed to protecting girls who become pregnant while still young: “These regions have begun to change because of the education we are providing through a special reproductive health campaign. Through our public education unit, we have prepared a guide for delivering correct family planning messages to various audiences.” ; says the campaigns also involve the use of the media to spread correct messages about safe use ; “We provide education to young people so that they have a broad understanding of the correct use of drugs and the various family planning methods. This has driven positive change in the southern regions and reduced teenage pregnancies.”

a6986.speaker: National Costed Implementation Plan for Family Planning 2019-2023 (Tanzania)
a6986.name: National Costed Implementation Plan for Family Planning 2019-2023 (Tanzania)
a6986.speech: Aims to strengthen family planning services, protect reproductive health rights and reduce unintended pregnancies, especially among young people and women; to increase the availability and use of family planning services, especially for young people and rural women; to prevent teenage and unintended pregnancies through education and youth-friendly services; to provide reproductive health education in schools and in the community; to put in place a policy and legal environment enabling access to services without stigma; and to increase collaboration among the private sector, civil society organisations and development partners.

a6986.speaker: Zawadi Ramadhani, reproductive health worker, Kitomanga health centre, Lindi Municipality
a6986.name: Zawadi Ramadhani
a6986.title: reproductive health worker, Kitomanga health centre, Lindi Municipality
a6986.speech: Says the limited understanding of some girls and parents is a challenge that causes the education not to be received properly ; says some girls feel ashamed to receive reproductive health education at health facilities, claiming these matters are for adults or those who are married ; says to address that challenge they have set a special schedule on Wednesdays and Saturdays for young people.

a7031.speaker: Maya Morsi, Egyptian Minister of Social Solidarity
a7031.name: Maya Morsi
a7031.title: Egyptian Minister of Social Solidarity
a7031.speech: Quoted by local media, praised the role of the Egyptian Red Crescent as the national mechanism responsible for distributing aid to Gaza, in accordance with international humanitarian law, stressing the consistency and effectiveness of its relief operations despite considerable challenges.

a7031.speaker: Mohamed Abdiker, Head of the International Organization for Migration (IOM)
a7031.name: Mohamed Abdiker
a7031.title: Head of the International Organization for Migration (IOM)
a7031.speech: Reaffirmed the IOM's commitment to intensifying cooperation with the Egyptian authorities through clear operational frameworks, in order to speed up the delivery of aid and to guarantee sustainable and coordinated humanitarian responses.

a7031.speaker: Mohamed Abdiker, Head of the International Organization for Migration (IOM)
a7031.name: Mohamed Abdiker
a7031.title: Head of the International Organization for Migration (IOM)
a7031.speech: Expressed his deep appreciation for Egypt's essential regional role in supporting Palestinians and Sudanese affected by humanitarian crises, commending the efforts of the Egyptian authorities in favour of peace and humanitarian aid.

a7429.speaker: Assiélou Felix Tanon, Ivorian Ambassador to Ghana
a7429.name: Assiélou Felix Tanon
a7429.title: Ivorian Ambassador to Ghana
a7429.speech: Said the two countries are on the verge of establishing the Ghana-La Côte d’Ivoire Chamber of Commerce to facilitate trade between Ghanaian and Ivorian enterprises ; described the recent bilateral successes as “marching towards prosperity together” ; emphasised that the two countries have had a long-standing relationship, with historical ties dating back to the medieval era, preparing an excellent opportunity for enhancing mutual benefits in various sectors, including security, economy, politics, trade and health ; stated, “the harmonious relation between the two countries has initiated a common interest towards the formation of the Ghana - Cote d’Ivoire Chamber of Commerce (GCCCI) to facilitate trade among Ghanaian and Ivorian businesses” ; said advanced consultations were ongoing between the Ivorian Embassy and the Ministry of Trade, Agribusiness & Industry, with a joint working committee formed to define operational modalities for establishing the GCCCI ; indicated that several companies from both countries, particularly in the agribusiness, logistics, construction, energy and financial services sectors, have expressed strong interest in the GCCCI and see the chamber as a strategic facilitator for business development and cross-investment consolidation ; argued that the Chamber of Commerce could play a key role in facilitating partnerships and reducing trade barriers between the two countries, thereby promoting increased bilateral trade, currently estimated at 311.9 billion FCFA in 2023, compared to 350.6 billion FCFA in 2022 ; added that Côte d’Ivoire mainly exports bulk cotton, processed cocoa, palm oil, iron, steel and steelwork, chemicals, textiles and footwear to Ghana, and imports fish, plastics, pharmaceuticals, vegetables, animal fats and oils and metal products from Ghana ; emphasised that Ghanaian and Ivorian businessmen and women rely on each other in export and import trades, hence there is a need to establish a joint chamber supported by a framework to boost trade between the two states.

a7429.speaker: Assiélou Felix Tanon, Ivorian Ambassador to Ghana
a7429.name: Assiélou Felix Tanon
a7429.title: Ivorian Ambassador to Ghana
a7429.speech: Affirmed that the two states could make history and be considered a twin state through trade ; expressed a wish for Cote d’Ivoire and Ghana to be pioneers in using the “Eco”, a currency that the ECOWAS considers as the medium of exchange, and for their cooperation to serve as an example for other countries.

a7429.speaker: Assiélou Felix Tanon, Ivorian Ambassador to Ghana
a7429.name: Assiélou Felix Tanon
a7429.title: Ivorian Ambassador to Ghana
a7429.speech: Underscored the collective gains that Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana have seen in recent years in the cocoa sector due to the La Côte d’Ivoire-Ghana Cocoa Initiative (CIGCI), also known as the Abidjan Declaration, established in 2018 ; emphasised that the two countries, which account for a combined 65 per cent of the world’s cocoa production, need to leverage their strength to demand a competitive price ; said the CIGCI allows the two leading producers of cocoa to speak with one voice on strategic issues, particularly fair remuneration for producers ; stated that the Living Income Differential (LID) mechanism, set at $400 per tonne, had fortified the West African countries’ position in global markets, whilst establishing the groundwork for enhanced economic justice for producers ; added, “A shared objective has been set to achieve at least 50 per cent local processing. Several measures are already in place, including creating and expanding industrial units, targeted tax incentives, logistics facilities and Public-Private Partnerships”.

a7488.speaker: Zuriel Oduwole, advocate for peace, education and gender equality, 2025 Nobel Peace Prize nominee
a7488.name: Zuriel Oduwole
a7488.title: advocate for peace, education and gender equality, 2025 Nobel Peace Prize nominee
a7488.speech: Upon learning of her Nobel Peace Prize nomination, expressed humility and surprise. “I have never sought recognition, only to speak up where it’s needed. This honour reflects the urgent need to invest in young voices as agents of change.”
